about: Ship sizing (RK3, Atomic Rockets plan section 5): the closed forms the ship designer sizes parts with, as named Equations. Thrust power, tanks and holds, crew room, the drive's waste heat and the radiators that shed it. The figures they read (stowage, room per person, waste share, radiator rule) are base-ships pack data.

checks.says: thrust must be zero or more, got {}
exhaust speed must be zero or more, got {}

references: Sutton, G. P. and Biblarz, O. 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th edn, Wiley, section 2.3 (jet power is half the mass flow times the exhaust speed squared, so half the thrust times the exhaust speed). https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Rocket+Propulsion+Elements%2C+9th+Edition-p-9781118753651

equation.name: How much power a drive's exhaust carries

source.text: Sutton and Biblarz 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements

explain.curious: A fast exhaust is expensive: the same push with twice the exhaust speed carries twice the power. That is why ion engines push so gently and torch drives need so much.
explain.science: Kinetic power of the exhaust stream: half the mass flow times v_e squared, and with F = mdot v_e that is F v_e / 2. Every power ledger checks a drive against it.

checks.says: mass must be zero or more, got {}

references: Halliday, D., Resnick, R. and Walker, J. 2013, Fundamentals of Physics, 10th edn, Wiley. chapter 14: density is mass over volume. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Fundamentals+of+Physics%2C+10th+Edition-p-9781118230718

equation.name: How much room a load takes

rho.name: how densely it packs (a liquid's density, or cargo's stowage)

source.text: Halliday, D., Resnick, R. and Walker, J. 2013, Fundamentals of Physics, 10th edn, Wiley

explain.curious: Hydrogen is so light that a tank of it is huge: a tonne of liquid hydrogen fills fourteen cubic metres, a tonne of water one.
explain.science: Volume of tanks and holds from the mass carried and its density: a propellant's liquid density from the data sheet, or the stowage factor of packed cargo.

checks.says: crew must be zero or more, got {}

references: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Revision B (2022), section 8.6 and Appendix F (net habitable volume per crew member). https://www.nasa.gov/reference/standard-3001/

equation.name: How much pressurised room a crew needs

g.name: share of a pressurised module left free once equipment and stowage are in

explain.curious: People need room to stay sane on long trips, and a module is only half free space once the kit is in.
explain.science: Pressurised volume from crew count, net habitable volume per person for the mission length, and the net-to-gross ratio of a module.

checks.says: waste per jet must be zero or more, got {}

references: Sutton, G. P. and Biblarz, O. 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th edn, Wiley, section 2.3 (jet power is half the mass flow times the exhaust speed squared, so half the thrust times the exhaust speed). https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Rocket+Propulsion+Elements%2C+9th+Edition-p-9781118753651

equation.name: How much heat a drive leaves on the ship

w.name: watts of heat left aboard for each watt in the jet

source.text: Sutton and Biblarz 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements

explain.curious: Any drive that is not perfectly efficient leaves heat behind, and in space the only way to lose it is to glow it away.
explain.science: Heat left aboard per watt of jet power: none for a chemical rocket (it leaves with the exhaust), large for reactor-driven and electric drives. The share is the drive family's figure in the base-ships pack.

checks.says: waste heat must be zero or more, got {}

references: Gilmore, D. G. (ed.) 2002, Spacecraft Thermal Control Handbook, Volume I, 2nd edn, The Aerospace Press, chapter 6 (radiators: heat rejected per face is emissivity times sigma T^4). doi:10.2514/4.989117

equation.name: How big the radiators must be

n.name: faces that see space (2 for a flat panel)

source.text: Gilmore 2002, Spacecraft Thermal Control Handbook, Volume I

explain.curious: Radiators grow fast as they cool: halve their temperature and they must be sixteen times bigger. Hot radiators are small; cool ones are vast.
explain.science: Panel area to reject the waste heat by thermal radiation alone, both faces radiating to cold space; sunlight and view factors are left out.

checks.says: tank pressure must be zero or more, got {}
volume must be zero or more, got {}

references: Young, W. C. and Budynas, R. G. 2002, Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 7th edn, McGraw-Hill, chapter 13 (thin-walled shells under internal pressure: the hoop stress is p r / t in a long cylinder and p r / 2t in a sphere, so the wall's mass is the shape factor times p V rho / sigma). https://openlibrary.org/isbn/007072542X
atoms.shown: m = φ p V ρ / σ

equation.name: How heavy a pressure tank's wall is
equation.formula: m = phi * p * V * rho / s

s.name: stress the wall may carry (strength over the safety factor)

phi.name: shape factor: 1.5 for a sphere, 2 for a long cylinder

source.text: Young and Budynas 2002, Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain

explain.curious: A tank's wall weighs in proportion to what it holds times how hard it is squeezed. Big tanks are not worse than small ones for pressure; a sphere is the lightest shape.
explain.science: Thin-wall membrane stress: the wall thickness that keeps hoop stress at the allowed value, times its area and density, is phi p V rho / sigma, independent of size. Ends, welds and fittings are left out.

checks.says: surface must be zero or more, got {}

references: Galilei, G. 1638, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, trans. Crew, H. and de Salvio, A. 1914, Dover reprint 1954, first day (bodies of one shape: their surfaces go as the squares and their volumes as the cubes of their size, so surface grows as the two-thirds power of volume). https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0486600998

equation.name: How much skin a load gains when split into tanks

A.name: surface of one tank holding it all

N.name: tanks of the same shape it is split into

S.name: surface of all the tanks together

explain.curious: Splitting a load into eight tanks doubles the skin round it. Insulation, sunshades and the cold that leaks in all grow with the skin, so many small tanks cost more than one big one.
explain.science: For similar shapes surface scales as volume to the two-thirds; N tanks of V/N each have N (V/N)^(2/3) = N^(1/3) V^(2/3), so N^(1/3) times the single tank's surface. Insulation mass and boil-off follow the surface.

references: Larson, W. J. and Wertz, J. R. (eds) 1999, Space Mission Analysis and Design, 3rd edn, Microcosm Press, chapter 13 (communications: a parabolic dish's gain is the aperture efficiency times (pi D / lambda)^2, and the link equation gives the data rate a received power supports at the needed energy per bit over the noise density). https://openlibrary.org/isbn/1881883108

equation.name: How much a dish concentrates a signal

eta.name: share of the dish that works (about 0.55)

G.name: gain over a bare antenna (as a ratio, not decibels)

source.text: Larson and Wertz 1999, Space Mission Analysis and Design

explain.curious: Double a dish's width and it throws four times as much of its signal at you. Shorter waves do the same, which is why deep-space links moved to higher bands.
explain.science: Directive gain of a filled circular aperture, 4 pi A_eff / lambda^2 with A_eff = eta pi D^2 / 4. Pointing loss and surface error are left to the efficiency.

atoms.shown: R = P G_t G_r (λ / 4π d)² / (k_B T_s (E_b/N₀))

equation.name: How fast a link can send
equation.formula: R = P * Gt * Gr * (lambda / (4 * pi * d)) ^ 2 / (k_B * T * E)

E.name: energy per bit over noise density the coding needs (as a ratio, not decibels)

R.name: data rate the link supports, in bits a second

source.text: Larson and Wertz 1999, Space Mission Analysis and Design

explain.curious: Twice as far, a quarter of the data. A probe at the edge of the system whispers; a bigger dish at either end, a stronger transmitter or a colder receiver buys the rate back.
explain.science: Friis free-space link: received power P Gt Gr (lambda / 4 pi d)^2 over the noise density k_B T_s and the needed Eb/N0 gives the bit rate. Pointing, air and line losses are left out.
